subject: HMC-NUTS in Nimble: Gradient of the Joint Posterior distribution or Conditional distribution ?

messages.author: 2db22d73ffad82a6
messages.subject: HMC-NUTS in Nimble: Gradient of the Joint Posterior distribution or Conditional distribution ?
parts:
Hi nimble community,

I am working on strategies to optimize MCMC efficiency in Nimble, particularly balancing mixing vs. computation time when applying HMC-NUTS to some specific selected parameters.

I understand that HMC is fundamentally based on the gradient of the log-joint posterior density. However, in Nimble, when specifying HMC-NUTS on a single parameter, the sampler operates within a Gibbs framework, where parameters are updated sequentially using their full conditional posterior distributions.

My question is:

  • Does HMC-NUTS in Nimble use the gradient of the full conditional P(θi∣data, all other parameters)?
  • Or does it still rely on the gradient of the full joint posterior (even when applied to a subset of parameters) ?

If it is the gradient of the joint posterior, does this mean the same gradient computation is performed, regardless of how many parameters we apply NUTS to?

Also, is there any Nimble instruction or any other way to inspect  how this gradient is computed for subgroups of parameters?

Thanks in advance for any insights!

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: HMC-NUTS in Nimble: Gradient of the Joint Posterior distribution or Conditional distribution ?
parts:
Hi Ro,

Thanks for the question.

The simple answer is that nimbleHMC's NUTS sampler uses the gradient of the full joint posterior. If you have assigned a NUTS sampler to a subset of parameters, then any dimensions of the full joint posterior that are not relevant to those parameters will not be included in the calculations, because they shouldn't matter.

If you want to catch the gradient calculation in action, I can give you a few suggestions. First, you can run nimbleHMC (or any of nimble's algorithms) uncompiled. I would only do this on a small toy model because it will be very slow. And the gradients then will be only numerical approximations using finite differences from package pracma or numDeriv. When running uncompiled, you can use R's debugging features to stop execution and be thrown into a browser wherever you'd like. To see where you might want to do this, take a look at the sampler_NUTS source code at nimbleHMC on GitHub.  Specifically, there is a method called `gradient`, which is called from `update_state_calcs`. (One thing that may be confusing is there is also a `gradient_aux` used for double-taping in the AD system.) Your question is really what is the function call for which the gradient is being taken. That is `calcLogProb(qArg)`, and internal to that the key step is `model$calculate(calcNodes)`. So if you inspect `calcNodes` (and check out the User Manual at r-nimble.org if you need to familiarize with "model$calculate"), you will see what model calculation the gradient is using. I have given a bit of gory detail because I got the impression you want to dig into how things work. 

After calling buildMCMC, you can access the sampler_NUTS object as an element of the samplerFunctions list in the object returned from buildMCMC.

You will also see various bits of code related to parameter transformation. HMC works best without constraints on the parameter space, so the parameter transformation system manages transformations to allow that where needed. It will be simpler for you to use a toy model with no constrained parameters and then the parameter transformation pieces will be trivial.

So for example, if you have done `MCMC <- buildMCMC(...)`, then you could do
MCMC$samplerFunctions[[1]]$calcNodes
to see the calcNodes and 
debug(MCMC$samplerFunctions[[1]]$calcLobProb)
to get into a browser every time the calcLogProb method is called (which will be a lot).

You also have the option of copying the sampler_NUTS source code to your own directory and making your own modified version of it. There may be some non-exported package functions in the setup code, and you can just preface those with "nimble:::" to access them.

Now if you want to stick your fingers into compiled execution, it is trickier. One option is to create a nimbleRcall to an R function in which you have a browser() statement (or have put it into debug mode). Then when the compiled code calls the nimbleRcall, you'll get an R prompt. At that point you are free to inspect or modify variables and/or call methods of the compiled model object as well as inspecting the compiled MCMC object.

If you want to access methods and variables inside the compiled sampler_NUTS from R, you need one more trick. The layers of interfacing that would be needed stop by default at one layer internal to any nimbleFunctions (otherwise they can get very cumbersome). To go deeper,  before compiling you can do:

nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions=TRUE)

Then if cMCMC is the compiled cMCMC you will be able to do

cMCMC$samplerFunctions[[1]]$state$gr_logProb for example to see the most recently calculated (and cached) gradient.

If you want to learn more about nimble's automatic differentiation system, there is a lot in the manual, and you could write a very small nimbleFunction based on sampler_NUTS that just takes a model and nodes and provides a gradient method.

I hope that helps get you started.

Perry

P.S. The term "Gibbs" can be a bit confusing because it refers to updates from full conditional distributions (using conjugate relationships among distributions, and always accepted) and is also associated with updating subsets of dimensions while holding others fixed. But even tools with "Gibbs" in the name aren't necessarily doing full conditional updates in all cases. We use a dialect of the BUGS language, but that doesn't mean the samplers are all conjugate. nimble does have such samplers (which we call conjugate to be more specific), but in general conjugacy doesn't hold and full conditionals are not available. So it is not the case that nimble uses Gibbs (conjugate) sampling in general. But it is the case that an MCMC kernel in nimble iterates over one or more samplers that can update one or more dimensions of a model. So, the way you started posing your question didn't really make sense to me.

parts:
Hi Perry,

Thank you very much for your detailed and insightful response! It clarifies several key aspects of how NUTS operates in NIMBLE, particularly regarding the gradient computation and how irrelevant dimensions are excluded when applying NUTS to a subset of parameters.

Your explanation about the distinction between Gibbs sampling and how NIMBLE handles parameter updates was also very helpful. I now understand that NIMBLE does not necessarily follow a strict Gibbs scheme in the sense of full conditional updates, which helps resolve some of my initial confusion.

I appreciate the debugging suggestions and will keep them in mind if I need to explore this further. Thanks again for your time and insights!

Best,
Ro
